passages.title: The shoe that rewrote the record books
passages.subtitle: How carbon plates and new foams changed distance running
passages.text:
When a group of distance runners lined up at the United States Olympic marathon trials in 2016, a few of them were wearing an unreleased prototype with a thick, slightly clumsy-looking sole. The shoe went on sale the following year as the Vaporfly 4%, and the number in its name was not decoration. It referred to the improvement its manufacturer said the shoe delivered in running economy — the quantity of oxygen an athlete burns to hold a given pace. Four per cent, in a sport where a leading marathon runner might hope to improve by a fraction of that in a year of training, was an extraordinary claim to print on a box.

Two components produced the effect. The first was the midsole, built from a light, highly resilient foam derived from a polymer family that had not previously been used for this purpose. Where the conventional midsole material of the previous three decades returned roughly sixty-five per cent of the energy an athlete put into each step, the new material returned something closer to eighty-five per cent, and it did so while weighing less. The second component sat inside that cushioning: a stiff, curved plate of carbon fibre, running almost the full length of the shoe.

Precisely how the plate works has proved harder to establish than the fact that it does. An early and intuitive explanation held that it acted as a spring, storing energy on landing and releasing it at push-off. Later work suggested something less romantic — that the plate mainly stiffens the joints of the toes, so the foot wastes less energy bending, and that it redistributes the load across the ankle and knee. A third account describes the plate and the sole together as a kind of see-saw that tips the runner forward. What researchers do broadly agree on is that neither element accounts for the result alone: the plate performs poorly without the foam around it, and the foam alone gives a smaller benefit than the pair together.

The four per cent figure itself came from a laboratory at the University of Colorado in Boulder, where runners were tested on treadmills while their oxygen consumption was recorded, allowing the researchers to calculate each athlete's running economy in one model of shoe after another. The average saving across the group was close to the advertised figure. The spread behind that average received far less attention. Some runners improved by barely two per cent; others gained more than six; a small number showed almost no measurable benefit at all. The shoe, in other words, does not do the same thing for everybody who puts it on.

At the elite level the results arrived quickly. In Vienna in October 2019, Eliud Kipchoge covered the marathon distance in under two hours. The run was never ratified as a record, because it used a rotating team of pacemakers and drinks were handed to him from a bicycle, but it was watched by an enormous audience and he ran it in a version of the shoe. Days later, Brigid Kosgei broke the women's world record in Chicago wearing the same technology. Within a season, the podium at almost every major marathon belonged to athletes in shoes of this type.

The reaction was not universally admiring. Critics argued that a gain of this size, available for the price of a shoe, amounted to technological doping, and that spectators could no longer tell how much of a performance belonged to the runner. Comparisons were drawn with competitive swimming, which had allowed full-body polyurethane suits, watched dozens of world records fall in a single season, and then banned them outright in 2010.

World Athletics, the sport's governing body, chose regulation rather than prohibition. Rules published at the start of 2020 capped the sole of a road-racing shoe at forty millimetres in thickness, permitted no more than one rigid plate within it, and required that any shoe worn in competition must have been on open sale to the public for at least four months. That last provision was aimed less at the technology than at access: it ended the practice of supplying unreleased prototypes to sponsored athletes alone.

The same principles soon reached the track, where spikes built around slimmer plates and the new foam preceded a run of fast times over distances from 1500 metres upwards. The rules that now exist set a ceiling rather than reversing anything, and every significant manufacturer sells a shoe designed to sit just beneath it. What has not been settled is the older question underneath the engineering: how much of what happens in a race should be credited to the athlete, and how much to the equipment they were given.

passages.title: The concrete that repairs itself
passages.subtitle: Why Roman harbours outlast modern ones
passages.text:
[A] At Baiae on the Bay of Naples the concrete piers of a Roman harbour still stand in the sea. They were poured before the birth of Christ, they have been under salt water ever since, and they are intact. A reinforced concrete jetty built in the same water in 1950 would by now have been condemned, patched, and probably demolished. This is an awkward comparison for an industry that produces the most heavily used manufactured substance on earth, and for most of the twentieth century it was treated as a curiosity rather than a question. It is a question.

[B] The recipe was never secret. Vitruvius, writing in the first century before Christ, set it out plainly: take the ash found in the region of Puteoli, mix it with lime and with rubble of volcanic rock, and it will set hard even under water. That ash, thrown out by the volcanic field west of Naples, is rich in silica and alumina in a glassy, chemically restless form. Lime alone will not harden under the sea. Lime combined with a reactive ash of this kind produces a binder that will, and Roman engineers used it to build harbours, breakwaters and fish tanks along the whole Mediterranean coast, shipping the ash by sea to sites that had no volcano of their own.

[C] What has since been discovered is that the sea, which destroys modern concrete, was doing the Roman material a favour. Seawater percolating slowly through the structure dissolves the volcanic glass that has not yet reacted, and from the dissolved material new minerals crystallise inside the pores and the cracks. The most important of them, a rare plate-like mineral called tobermorite, is almost impossible to grow deliberately in a laboratory at ordinary temperatures, yet it forms unhurried in these piers over centuries. Its interlocking plates reinforce the binder from the inside. A Roman breakwater does not merely resist the sea; it uses the sea to go on assembling itself, and is stronger after two thousand years than it was after twenty.

[D] A second mechanism was identified only recently, and it explains something that had been dismissed as sloppy workmanship. Roman concrete is full of small white lumps of lime, which archaeologists long assumed were the result of careless mixing. Careful examination showed instead that the lime had been added unslaked and mixed hot, at temperatures that leave these lumps deliberately scattered through the material. They are reservoirs. When a crack opens and water reaches one, the lump dissolves and the solution recrystallises in the crack as calcite, sealing it. The material repairs its own fractures, which is precisely the failure mode that ends the life of a modern structure.

[E] Modern concrete fails for a reason the Romans never had to consider, because they never used steel. Portland cement is strong in compression and feeble in tension, so since the nineteenth century it has been cast around steel bars that carry the tensile load. The arrangement works until salt or carbon dioxide reaches the steel. The bars then rust, rust occupies more volume than the metal it replaces, and the expansion splits the concrete from within, opening paths for more salt to arrive. The very component that makes the modern material useful is the component that limits its life, and no improvement to the cement itself can remove that vulnerability.

[F] None of which means the ancient recipe should simply be revived. Roman concrete is weak in tension too, and without reinforcement it cannot span or cantilever, so it could not produce a bridge deck, a multi-storey frame or anything else that defines modern construction. It gains its strength slowly, over months and years rather than the days a construction programme allows. It depends on a volcanic ash of a particular composition that is abundant near Naples and absent almost everywhere else. What the Roman harbours offer is not a blueprint but a demonstration that durability of this order is chemically possible.

[G] The reason anyone is paying attention now is the carbon arithmetic. Making Portland cement requires heating limestone to around fourteen hundred degrees, which burns fuel and drives carbon dioxide out of the rock itself, and the industry is responsible for a share of global emissions larger than aviation and shipping combined. Replacing part of the cement with a reactive ash cuts that figure directly, and blends using fly ash from coal power stations or slag from steelworks already do so. Both supplies are shrinking as the industries that produced them close down. The search has therefore turned to the material the Romans used, and to the harder problem the piers at Baiae pose: how to build something that lasts long enough that it does not have to be built twice.

passages.title: The case against the smart city
passages.subtitle: What the sensors are actually being asked to solve
passages.text:
Every few years a city is offered the same proposal. Instrument the streets with sensors, gather the resulting data in a central platform, and let software allocate the traffic, the energy, the rubbish collection and the policing more efficiently than the municipality has managed on its own. The pitch is delivered with renderings of clean plazas and is rarely accompanied by a figure for what any of it costs to run. It is worth asking why a proposal this attractive has produced so little.

The purpose-built examples are not encouraging. Songdo in South Korea was designed from empty reclaimed land as a fully instrumented city and has spent more than a decade struggling to attract the residents its plans assumed. Masdar in the United Arab Emirates was to be a carbon-neutral settlement of fifty thousand people and remains, long past its original completion date, a small research campus. The most instructive case is the one that never began: a proposal by a subsidiary of Google to develop a district of the Toronto waterfront, which collapsed in 2020 after two years of public argument that was not really about technology at all. It was about who would hold the data, who had authorised its collection, and what recourse a resident would have. The company withdrew without those questions being answered.

The recurring flaw is a category error. The difficulties that actually afflict cities are overwhelmingly political, and they are presented as though they were informational. Traffic congestion is the standard illustration. It is not caused by drivers lacking information about traffic; it is caused by a large number of people wanting to occupy the same scarce road space at the same moment, at a price that does not reflect its scarcity. A city that prices road space, or that converts a lane to buses, will reduce congestion. A city that installs sensors to measure congestion in finer detail will know more about it. Only one of those is a solution, and the difference is that the first requires a council to face down an organised constituency while the second requires a procurement.

Procurement brings its own problem. These platforms are proprietary, and a municipality that runs its transport, lighting and waste systems on one supplier's software cannot readily change supplier, because the cost of migrating is deliberately high and the expertise to do it sits with the vendor rather than with the city. Local authorities have spent thirty years reducing their internal technical capacity; they are now poorly placed to specify such systems, audit them, or take them back. A dependency of this kind is not a partnership. It is the transfer of a core municipal function to a company whose obligations end at the contract.

Then there is the ratchet. Data gathered for one stated purpose does not stay there, because a system that already exists is far easier to point at a new problem than a system that must be built and justified from nothing. Cameras installed to time traffic signals become cameras that enforce parking, then cameras that support investigations, and each step is individually reasonable and collectively a surveillance infrastructure that no one ever voted to build. The safeguard usually offered is a policy document, which is to say a promise by the present administration about the behaviour of its successors.

A subtler objection concerns what optimisation actually optimises. A system trained on how a city is currently used will efficiently reproduce how a city is currently used. If a neighbourhood has poor bus service, the demand data will show few bus passengers there, and a model allocating vehicles by demand will conclude that few are needed. The existing pattern is read as a preference rather than as a consequence of past decisions, and the algorithm hardens it. Efficiency, applied without a view about what the city ought to become, is a machine for entrenching the status quo with better graphics.

None of this is an argument against technology in city government, and the record here is genuinely positive — it is simply unexciting. Acoustic sensors placed on water mains locate leaks that would otherwise run for months, and cities using them have cut losses substantially. Traffic signals that adapt to actual queues rather than to a fixed timetable move buses through junctions measurably faster. These systems share a shape. Each addresses a narrow, well-defined problem, produces a result that can be checked against a number the city already collects, and runs on equipment that can be replaced by a different supplier next year. None of them requires a district to be rebuilt, and none of them appears in a rendering.

That suggests a test any council could apply before signing. Would this still be worth doing if the data it generates were published openly, and if the supplier could be replaced at the end of the term without the system ceasing to function? A proposal that survives both conditions is probably a piece of useful municipal infrastructure. A proposal that fails either one is not selling a city a capability. It is selling the city a landlord.
